_readme: Cross-language conformance fixture for the tab-title cleaning rule.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: every writer of a tab title cleans it -- the worker at the three
title-writing RPCs (OpenAgent, RenameAgent, UpdateTerminalTitle) and at the plan
auto-rename, and the browser at the inline rename it sends them. No path refuses a
title. That only holds if the two implementations clean IDENTICALLY: the browser
patches its own tab metadata optimistically, so a rule that drifts leaves the tab strip
showing one title while the worker stores another, with no error anywhere to say so.
This file is the check: both suites read it, so EDITING ONE SIDE WITHOUT THE OTHER IS
THE EXACT BUG IT PREVENTS -- the language that drifts is the one whose CI turns red.
THE RULE, in order: strip what a reader cannot see, fold each run of whitespace to one
space, trim both ends, then cut to 128 UTF-8 BYTES at a character boundary and trim
again. The order is CLEAN FIRST, CUT SECOND. Do not reverse it. Cutting last makes the
result fit the limit by construction, whatever the strip did, and it keeps the text the
user typed. The 'leading invisible characters do not remove the title' case below is
what a cut-first rule got wrong. The second trim is for the cut that lands on the space
between two words.
WHAT THE STRIP REMOVES: three classes. The control blocks U+0000-U+001F and
U+007F-U+009F, which is the whole Cc category that Go's unicode.IsControl reports --
EXCEPT U+0009-U+000D and U+0085, which are control characters AND whitespace at the same
time and reach THE FOLD instead. The invisible format characters: the soft hyphen, the
zero width space, the word joiner, the bidirectional marks and overrides and isolates,
and U+FEFF. A lone surrogate, and an invalid byte. The strip removes
NOTHING ELSE. A quote, a backslash, a dollar and a percent are ordinary text: no sink
reads a stored title as syntax, because the shell path quotes each argument, the
stylesheet path escapes at the emitter, and the plan file name keeps letters and digits
only. U+200C and U+200D stay, because the joiner builds an emoji family and both shape a
word in Indic, Persian and Arabic orthography; the variation selectors stay for the same
reason.
THE FOLD SET IS PINNED BY CODE POINT, on both sides, and this is why. Go's
unicode.IsSpace reads a table that moves with the Go release, and JavaScript's \s reads
one that moves with the engine, so a Space_Separator added to Unicode later would reach
the worker and the browser in DIFFERENT WEEKS: one side folds a character the other
keeps. The Cc category is frozen, so the strip was already deterministic; the fold was
the last half of this rule that two runtimes could answer differently. Both sides now
hold the same 25 code points: U+0009-U+000D, U+0020, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680,
The pin costs staleness ON PURPOSE. A Space_Separator added later is NOT folded and
renders as a visible character inside a title, on both sides, until somebody adds it to
both lists and writes a case here. That failure is visible; the drift it replaces was
silent. TestNameWhitespaceMatchesUnicode in Go and the 'pinned whitespace set' block in
TypeScript each compare the pinned set against their own runtime and report the day it
moves, so the staleness is a decision somebody makes rather than one that happens.
The 25 characters are Go's unicode.IsSpace, which is \s with exactly two edits. U+0085
is IN, because Go claims it and \s does not. U+FEFF is OUT, because \s claims it and Go
does not -- and the strip removes U+FEFF before the fold reads the string anyway. The 'a
next line folds' case pins the first edit; the two U+FEFF cases pin the second. The 'a
no-break space folds' case pins the rest of the shared set.
The unit is BYTES on both sides, because Go's `len` counts bytes. 128 bytes is 128
ASCII characters but only 42 CJK characters, so a character count and a byte count
disagree on every wider script -- the '50 CJK characters' case is 50 characters and 150
bytes. The cut also has to land on a character boundary in both languages:
String.prototype.slice counts UTF-16 code units and splits a surrogate pair in half, so
the 'cut lands inside a surrogate pair' case is what refuses that shortcut.
NOT HERE, and it cannot be: the invalid-byte and lone-surrogate cases. encoding/json
rewrites an unpaired \uD800 escape to U+FFFD, so this file cannot carry such an input at
all -- the fixture would pin the replacement character rather than the case. Each
language pins its own half instead: TestCleanNameDropsInvalidBytes in Go, and the
'drops a lone surrogate' case in the TypeScript suite.
CONSUMED BY (keep both in sync with this schema):
Go: backend/util/validate/name_test.go   TestCleanNameConformance
TS: frontend/src/lib/validate.test.ts    cleanName conformance block
THE CONTRACT, per case: `input` and `cleaned` are both SPECS, and a spec builds one
string as `text` repeated `repeat` times followed by `tail` (an ABSENT `repeat` means 1,
an explicit `"repeat": 0` means zero copies, and `text` and `tail` default to the empty
string). Both loaders tell an absent `repeat` from an explicit 0, so an explicit 0 builds
the same string in both languages. The spec exists so a boundary reads as
the NUMBER 128 rather than as 128 characters a reader has to count. Both sides assert:
clean(build(input))   == build(cleaned)
clean(build(cleaned)) == build(cleaned)   -- idempotence, for every case
`why` is documentation only; neither suite asserts on it.
Every character outside printable ASCII is written as an escape, so this file states
which code point each case means and stays readable in a diff.

cases.why: an already clean title passes through unchanged
an empty title cleans to empty -- each caller supplies its own fallback
the whitespace at both ends is trimmed
a C0 control character (NUL) is stripped and the rest of the title survives
the C1 block is control too: Go's unicode.IsControl covers U+0080-U+009F, so the browser regex has to cover it as well
a quote, a backslash, a dollar and a percent are ordinary text and survive
a shell command used as a background-task label keeps every character it needs
a Windows path used as a terminal title keeps its backslashes

a LEADING U+FEFF is stripped. JS trim() removes it and Go TrimSpace keeps it, so a pasted byte order mark was the one input on which the two rules disagreed. This case pins the Go half, where the strip is what removes it
a U+FEFF in the MIDDLE is stripped too. No trim reaches it on either side, so this case pins BOTH halves: the character rule has to name U+FEFF, not lean on the trim
a zero width space and a soft hyphen are invisible, so both are stripped
a right-to-left override is stripped: it reorders what the tab strip renders, which is how one name is made to read as another
the bidi isolates are stripped, and the space that survives is folded normally
the word joiner is stripped: it occupies no width
U+200D is KEPT: stripping the zero width joiner would break the emoji family into three separate people
a variation selector is KEPT: U+FE0F is what makes the character render as an emoji rather than as its text form
a newline FOLDS to one space rather than vanishing, so the two words do not run together
a tab folds to one space the same way
a run of spaces folds to one
a no-break space folds to a plain space: this is where Go's unicode.IsSpace and JavaScript's \s have to agree

a next line (U+0085) FOLDS on both sides, and it is the ONE character Go's unicode.IsSpace claims and JavaScript's \s does not. Go reaches the fold because the whitespace test runs before the control test; the browser reaches it because NAME_INVISIBLE_G excludes \x85 and NAME_WHITESPACE_G names it. Remove either and this case is what turns red
a vertical tab folds too. It sits inside the U+0009-U+000D gap that the browser strip class punches by hand, so this case and the next pin both ends of that gap
a form feed folds, which pins the far end of the same gap

the invisible math operators are KEPT. They occupy no width, so the rule arguably should strip them, and it does not -- the set is a curated list rather than a category test. This case states the current answer so a change to it is deliberate and lands on both sides at once
a title that used to clean to EMPTY now keeps its characters, and only the whitespace run folds
a title of nothing but control characters still cleans to empty -- the caller's fallback case
exactly 128 bytes: the limit is inclusive, so nothing is cut
129 bytes: one byte over, so one byte goes
50 CJK characters is 150 bytes: under a 128-CHARACTER cap and over the 128-BYTE one. The cut at byte 128 lands inside the 43rd character, so it moves back to 126 bytes
32 emoji is exactly 128 bytes (4 each): an astral character that sits on the limit is kept whole

the cut lands inside a surrogate pair: 30 units of 5 bytes is 150 bytes, and byte 128 sits in the 26th emoji, so the whole emoji goes and 126 bytes remain. A UTF-16 slice(0,128) keeps half a pair here
the cut leaves a trailing space, which the second trim then removes -- the trim runs AFTER the cut
130 invisible characters do not remove the title: the strip runs BEFORE the cut, so `Plan` is what reaches the 128-byte limit. A cut-first rule returned the empty string here
the cut runs LAST and it counts kept characters: 132 bytes of ordinary text lose the final four
120 bytes of CJK plus a dollar: 121 bytes, so nothing is cut and nothing is stripped
